description:
FILED s473e (Opus, 2026-09-08) while shipping #1244 (b).  PRE-EXISTING, and
independent of loop control: perl clears `$@` when it ENTERS an eval, PCL only
sets it when the eval LEAVES.  So the previous error is visible inside the eval
body, and it survives any exit that is not a normal return.

PROBE (perl 5.40.3 vs PCL at s473e's tree), scratch/s473e/p/m2d.pl:

    eval { die "old\n" };
    eval { print "in-block=[$@]\n" };
    eval { die "old2\n" };
    eval q{ print "in-string=[$@]\n" };

  perl:  in-block=[]        in-string=[]
  PCL:   in-block=[old\n]   in-string=[old2\n]

and the exit-shaped consequence (scratch/s473e/p/m2c.pl):

    eval { die "old\n" };
    my $k=0; for my $i (1..3) { $k++; eval q{last}; $k+=100 }
    print "k=$k after=[$@]\n";

  perl:  k=1 after=[]
  PCL:   k=1 after=[old\n]      (k is right since s473e; $@ is stale)

WHERE.  Two sites, both of which set `$@` only on the way out:
  * `%p-eval-1` (string eval) -- `(box-set $@ "")` sits after the body inside
    the handler-case's success arm;
  * `p-eval-block` -- the `prog1`'s second form.
Neither clears on entry, and neither runs at all when the body is left by a
non-local exit (a loop-control throw, a `last` out of an enclosing loop).

THE FIX is one `(box-set $@ "")` at the head of each, before the body.  It was
NOT done in s473e because it is a separate mechanism with a much wider blast
radius than the loop-control work it was found beside: every program that reads
`$@` inside an eval body changes answer, so it needs its own full sweep and its
own probe battery (nested evals, `$@` read by a `local $SIG{__DIE__}` handler,
`p-try`'s own localisation, and whether the clear belongs before or after the
`$^S` bind).  `docs/ir-spec.md` does not state the rule either way today.

WHAT NOT TO RETRY: do not "fix" this by clearing `$@` at the loop-control throw
site -- the divergence is not about loop control at all (the `in-block` probe
above has no loop in it).
subject: PCL sets $@ only when an eval LEAVES; perl clears it when the eval is ENTERED, so a previous error is visible inside the eval body and survives a non-local exit out of it
